questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A rectangular block of a metal measures 1 cm × 2 cm × 4 cm. Its resistance is measured between each pair of opposite faces in turn, the current being spread uniformly over the two faces used. The ratio of the largest of these three resistances to the smallest is:

solution.concept: R = ρl/A: the resistance is largest for the longest current path through the smallest cross-section
solution.explanation: The resistivity is fixed by the material. Between the 1 cm × 2 cm faces the current path is 4 cm long through an area of 2 cm²; between the 2 cm × 4 cm faces the path is 1 cm long through 8 cm².
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 uses only the ratio of the lengths (or only the ratio of the face areas); both change together. 64 cubes the length ratio. 1/16 is the smallest-to-largest ratio, inverted.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Ohm's law; resistivity (R = ρl/A)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An electric heater rated 2.0 kW is used for 3 hours every day. The electrical energy it consumes in 30 days is:

solution.concept: Electrical energy = power × time; 1 kWh is the energy used by a 1 kW appliance in 1 hour
solution.explanation: The heater uses 2.0 kW for 3 h each day, i.e. 6 kWh a day, for 30 days.
steps: Energy per day = 2.0 kW × 3 h = 6.0 kWh
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.0 kWh is the energy for a single day. 60 kWh leaves out the 3 hours a day. 1.8 × 10⁵ kWh puts the power in watts (2000 W) but keeps the unit kWh.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electrical energy, power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A cell is supplying a steady current to an external resistor. Inside the cell (through its electrolyte), the conventional current flows:

options.text: from the positive terminal to the negative terminal
in neither direction, because current flows only in the external circuit
from the negative terminal to the positive terminal
from the positive terminal to the negative terminal, but only if the internal resistance is negligible

solution.concept: A cell is a source of emf: inside it, charges are driven against the electrostatic field
solution.explanation: In a steady circuit the current is the same all round the closed loop. In the external resistor the conventional current goes from the positive terminal to the negative terminal, so to complete the loop it must go from the negative terminal to the positive terminal inside the cell. The chemical action of the cell does the work of moving the charges this way, against the electrostatic field.
steps: Steady current: same current all round the closed loop
Outside: positive terminal → resistor → negative terminal
Inside the cell: negative terminal → positive terminal
solution.why_others_wrong: The positive-to-negative direction holds only in the external circuit (or inside a cell that is being charged). Current does flow through the cell, which is part of the closed loop. The internal resistance does not decide the direction of the current inside the cell.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance
solution.final_answer: Option C: from the negative terminal to the positive terminal

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a closed loop ABCDA of a circuit carrying steady currents, the potential falls by 5 V from A to B (across a resistor), rises by 12 V from B to C (across a cell) and falls by 3 V from C to D (across another resistor). The change in potential from D back to A is:

solution.concept: Kirchhoff's loop rule: the algebraic sum of the changes in potential round any closed loop is zero
solution.explanation: Going once round the loop brings us back to the starting point, so all the changes of potential must add up to zero: −5 + 12 − 3 + ΔV_DA = 0.
steps: −5 V + 12 V − 3 V = +4 V from A to D
ΔV_DA = −4 V, i.e. a fall of 4 V
solution.why_others_wrong: A rise of 4 V has the sign wrong: the potential has already risen by 4 V from A to D, so it must fall by 4 V on the way back. 20 V adds the magnitudes of the three changes and ignores their signs. Zero would hold only if the first three changes already summed to zero.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Kirchhoff's rules
solution.final_answer: Option D: a fall of 4 V

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform wire of resistance 16 Ω is bent into the shape of a square, its two ends being joined. The resistance between two adjacent corners of the square is:

solution.concept: Parallel combination of the two paths between the chosen points
solution.explanation: Each side has a resistance of 16/4 = 4 Ω. Between two adjacent corners there are two paths in parallel: one side (4 Ω) and the other three sides in series (12 Ω).
steps: Paths: 4 Ω and 12 Ω in parallel
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 Ω takes only the single side and ignores the parallel path round the other three sides. 12 Ω takes only the longer path. 16 Ω is the resistance of the whole straight wire.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors - series and parallel

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For a metallic conductor, the potential difference across it is proportional to the current through it only so long as its temperature and other physical conditions remain unchanged.
Statement II: When a uniform wire is cut into two equal halves, the resistivity of the material of each half is half that of the original wire.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Ohm's law and the difference between resistance and resistivity
solution.explanation: Statement I is true: Ohm's law, V = IR with R constant, holds for a metal only when its temperature (and other physical conditions) do not change; heating the conductor changes its resistance. Statement II is false: resistivity is a property of the material at a given temperature and does not depend on the dimensions of the wire. Cutting the wire halves its resistance, not its resistivity.
steps: I: R constant only at fixed temperature → true
II: ρ depends on material and temperature, not size → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II confuses resistivity with resistance, which is the quantity that halves.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Ohm's law; resistivity of various materials
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A metal has one free electron per atom. Its density is 9.0 × 10³ kg m⁻³ and its molar mass is 60 g mol⁻¹. A wire of this metal, of cross-sectional area 1.0 mm², carries a steady current of 7.2 A. Taking Avogadro's number as 6.0 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the drift speed of the free electrons is:

solution.concept: Number density of free electrons from density and molar mass; I = neAv_d
solution.explanation: One cubic metre of the metal has a mass of 9.0 × 10³ kg = 150 mol, i.e. 150 × 6.0 × 10²³ = 9.0 × 10²⁸ atoms, and so 9.0 × 10²⁸ free electrons. The drift speed then follows from I = neAv_d.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.50 m/s uses the molar mass as 60 kg mol⁻¹ (grams not converted), making n 1000 times too small. 0.25 mm/s assumes two free electrons per atom. 8.3 mm/s multiplies the density by N_A without dividing by the molar mass.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Wire P has a resistance of 10 Ω at 0 °C and a temperature coefficient of resistance of 4.0 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹. Wire Q has a resistance of 12 Ω at 0 °C and a temperature coefficient of resistance of 2.0 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹. Both coefficients are referred to 0 °C and may be taken as constant. The temperature at which the two wires have equal resistances is:

solution.concept: R_t = R₀(1 + αt) for each wire
solution.explanation: Wire P starts with the smaller resistance but its resistance rises faster. Equate the two expressions and solve for t.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 °C lets only P's resistance change (10(1 + 0.004t) = 12). 100 °C and 83 °C multiply the difference of the two coefficients by a single base resistance (10 Ω or 12 Ω), instead of using 10α_P − 12α_Q.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', temperature dependence of resistivity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: To measure an unknown resistance R, it is connected in series with an ammeter of resistance 0.50 Ω, and a voltmeter is connected across the series combination of R and the ammeter. The voltmeter reads 5.0 V and the ammeter reads 0.50 A. The value of R is:

solution.concept: Ohm's law applied to the part of the circuit across which the voltmeter is connected
solution.explanation: The voltmeter measures the potential difference across R and the ammeter together, and the ammeter reading is the current through both. So V/I is the total resistance R + R_A.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 Ω ignores the resistance of the ammeter, which is inside the voltmeter's connections. 10.5 Ω adds the ammeter resistance instead of subtracting it. 9.75 Ω subtracts the ammeter's potential drop (0.25 V) as if it were a resistance in ohms.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Ohm's law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A battery of emf 12 V delivers exactly the same power to an external resistor of 2 Ω as to an external resistor of 8 Ω (each connected alone across it). The internal resistance of the battery and the power delivered in either case are, respectively:

solution.concept: Power in the external resistor P = ε²R/(R + r)²
solution.explanation: Equating the power for R₁ = 2 Ω and R₂ = 8 Ω gives R₁(R₂ + r)² = R₂(R₁ + r)², which simplifies to r² = R₁R₂.
solution.shortcut: Equal power in R₁ and R₂ means r = √(R₁R₂).
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 Ω is the arithmetic mean of 2 Ω and 8 Ω; the condition gives the geometric mean. 9 W is the maximum power ε²/4r, delivered only when R = r = 4 Ω, not in these two cases. 6 Ω (the difference 8 − 2) does not make the two powers equal.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance; electrical energy, power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two resistors are connected first in series and then in parallel across the same ideal battery. The total power drawn from the battery in the parallel arrangement is 4.5 times that drawn in the series arrangement. The ratio of the larger resistance to the smaller resistance is:

solution.concept: For a fixed voltage, P = V²/R_eq, so P_parallel/P_series = R_series/R_parallel
solution.explanation: Let the resistances be R and xR. Then R_series = R(1 + x) and R_parallel = Rx/(1 + x), so the power ratio is (1 + x)²/x.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.5 takes the power ratio itself as the resistance ratio. A ratio of 1 (equal resistors) gives a power ratio of 4, and a ratio of 3 gives 16/3 ≈ 5.3, not 4.5.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors - series and parallel; electrical energy, power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An electric kettle draws a power of 1.0 kW from the mains. It heats 1.0 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C, and 80% of the electrical energy it draws goes into heating the water. Taking the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, the time taken is:

solution.concept: Electrical energy = Pt; only the useful fraction of it heats the water
solution.explanation: Heat needed by the water = mcΔT. The kettle supplies 1000 J each second, of which only 800 J reaches the water.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.6 min ignores the 80% efficiency. 4.5 min multiplies by 0.80 instead of dividing by it. 8.75 min takes the temperature rise as 100 °C instead of 80 °C.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electrical energy, power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a constant potential difference is applied across a metal wire, the current in it settles at a steady value, even though the electric field accelerates each free electron between collisions.
Reason (R): Collisions with the ions of the metal keep randomising the velocities of the electrons, so the average velocity they acquire in the field, the drift velocity eEτ/m, does not keep growing with time.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Drift velocity: acceleration between collisions, randomisation at collisions
solution.explanation: Between collisions each electron is accelerated by the field, but after a collision its velocity is random again. Averaged over all electrons, the velocity gained is the acceleration eE/m times the average time τ since the last collision, which is a constant. A constant drift velocity means a constant current I = neAv_d. R gives exactly this reason, so it explains A.
steps: A: steady current for a fixed potential difference → true
R: collisions randomise velocities; v_d = eEτ/m is constant → true
R explains why the current does not keep increasing → A
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, and the constant drift velocity of R is the reason why the current in A is steady.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A cell of emf ε and internal resistance r is connected across an external resistor R. Match each quantity in List-I with its expression in List-II.

List-I:
A. Current in the circuit
B. Potential difference across the terminals of the cell
C. Power delivered to the external resistor
D. Fraction of the power generated by the cell that is delivered to the external resistor

List-II:
I. εR/(R + r)
II. R/(R + r)
III. ε/(R + r)
IV. ε²R/(R + r)²

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Cell with internal resistance: I = ε/(R + r), V = IR, P = I²R
solution.explanation: The current is ε/(R + r). The terminal potential difference is V = ε − Ir = IR = εR/(R + r). The power in R is I²R = ε²R/(R + r)². The cell generates power εI, of which I²R reaches R, so the fraction is IR/ε = R/(R + r).
solution.why_others_wrong: The code with B-II, D-I interchanges the terminal voltage (which carries ε) and the dimensionless fraction. A-I, B-III interchanges the current and the terminal voltage. C-II, D-IV gives a dimensionless ratio as a power.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance; electrical energy, power
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Four identical cells, each of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω, are meant to be connected in parallel (all positive terminals joined together and all negative terminals joined together), but one of them is connected the wrong way round. A 0.5 Ω resistor is connected across the two common terminals. The current through the resistor is:

solution.concept: Kirchhoff's junction rule at the common terminal (or the equivalent cell of a parallel group)
solution.explanation: Let V be the potential of the common positive line relative to the common negative line. Each correctly connected cell sends (1.5 − V)/0.5 into the line; the reversed cell sends (−1.5 − V)/0.5; together these must equal the current V/0.5 through the resistor.
solution.shortcut: Equivalent cell: emf = (1.5 + 1.5 + 1.5 − 1.5)/4 = 0.75 V, internal resistance 0.5/4 = 0.125 Ω; I = 0.75/0.625 = 1.2 A.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.4 A takes all four cells as correctly connected. 0.75 A uses the right equivalent emf but the internal resistance of one cell (0.5 Ω) instead of r/4. 2.25 A simply leaves the reversed cell out of the circuit.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells in series and in parallel

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a circuit, points A and B are connected to a common return line G as follows. Between G and A: a cell of emf 12 V and internal resistance 1 Ω, its positive terminal towards A. Between A and G: a 4 Ω resistor. Between A and B: a 2 Ω resistor. Between B and G: a 2 Ω resistor and, in parallel with it, a cell of emf 4 V and internal resistance 1 Ω, its positive terminal towards B. The current through the 4 V cell is:

options.text: 4 A, out of its positive terminal

solution.concept: Kirchhoff's rules (junction rule at A and B) for a network with two cells
solution.explanation: Take G as 0 V and let the potentials of A and B be V_A and V_B. The junction rule at A and at B gives two equations. Solving them, the potential of B comes out equal to 4 V, the emf of the second cell, so no current flows through that cell.
steps: Check: 4 A from the 12 V cell = 2 A (4 Ω) + 2 A (A to B); 2 A from A to B all goes through the 2 Ω to G
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 A is the current through the 2 Ω resistor between A and B (and through the 2 Ω between B and G), not through the cell. 4 A is the current through the 12 V cell. 1 A would need the potential of B to be 3 V or 5 V, which does not satisfy the junction rule at B.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Kirchhoff's rules

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two 1.0 kΩ resistors R₁ and R₂ are connected in series across an ideal 12 V battery. A voltmeter connected across R₁ reads 4.0 V. The resistance of the voltmeter is:

solution.concept: A voltmeter of finite resistance in parallel with a resistor; series current shared at the junction
solution.explanation: With the voltmeter connected, the p.d. across R₂ is 12 − 4 = 8 V, so the current through R₂ (and from the battery) is 8 mA. Only 4.0/1000 = 4 mA of this goes through R₁; the remaining 4 mA goes through the voltmeter, which has 4.0 V across it.
steps: Current through R₂ = 8.0 V/1.0 kΩ = 8.0 mA
Current through R₁ = 4.0 V/1.0 kΩ = 4.0 mA
Voltmeter current = 8.0 − 4.0 = 4.0 mA → R_V = 4.0 V/4.0 mA = 1.0 kΩ
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.50 kΩ (4 V/8 mA) is the resistance of R₁ and the voltmeter in parallel, not of the voltmeter alone. 2.0 kΩ divides the 8 V across R₂ by the voltmeter current. 3.0 kΩ divides the battery emf by the voltmeter current.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors - series and parallel; Kirchhoff's rules

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A Wheatstone bridge with unequal resistances P and Q in one branch (P/Q = R/S) remains balanced if P and Q alone are interchanged.
Statement II: The balance condition of a Wheatstone bridge is obtained by applying Kirchhoff's loop rule to two loops, together with the condition that no current flows through the galvanometer.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Wheatstone bridge: balance condition and its derivation
solution.explanation: Statement I is false: after the interchange the ratio in that branch becomes Q/P, which differs from R/S unless P = Q, so the galvanometer deflects. Statement II is true: with I_g = 0, the loop rule applied to the loop containing P, the galvanometer and R, and to the loop containing Q, the galvanometer and S, gives I₁P = I₂R and I₁Q = I₂S, whose ratio is P/Q = R/S.
steps: I: Q/P ≠ R/S when P ≠ Q → false
II: loop rule + I_g = 0 gives P/Q = R/S → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Interchanging P with Q inverts their ratio; a balanced bridge stays balanced under such a swap only in the special case P = Q.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Wheatstone bridge
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): By connecting more and more identical cells in parallel across a fixed external resistor, the current through the resistor can be made as large as we please.
Reason (R): The internal resistance of n identical cells, each of internal resistance r, connected in parallel is r/n.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Parallel grouping of cells: emf unchanged, internal resistance divided by n
solution.explanation: For n identical cells in parallel the emf stays ε and the internal resistance is r/n, so the current is I = ε/(R + r/n). As n grows, r/n tends to zero and I approaches ε/R, but never exceeds it. So the current is limited and A is false. R is true.
steps: I = ε/(R + r/n) → ε/R as n → ∞
A: the current cannot exceed ε/R → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Adding cells in parallel never raises the emf, so the current is bounded by ε/R; A is false while R is a correct statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells in series and in parallel
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Two bulbs, rated 100 W, 220 V and 25 W, 220 V, are connected in series across a 440 V supply. Treat the resistance of each bulb as constant, equal to the value implied by its rating. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The resistance of the 25 W bulb is four times that of the 100 W bulb.
(b) The current in the circuit is about 0.18 A.
(c) The potential difference across the 25 W bulb is about 352 V, well above its rated voltage.
(d) The 100 W bulb dissipates more power than the 25 W bulb.
(e) The power dissipated in the 100 W bulb is about 16 W.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Rated values give R = V²/P; in series the same current flows and the voltage divides in the ratio of resistances
solution.explanation: R(100 W) = 220²/100 = 484 Ω and R(25 W) = 220²/25 = 1936 Ω. In series across 440 V the current is 440/2420 ≈ 0.18 A. The voltage divides as 1 : 4, so 88 V across the 100 W bulb and 352 V across the 25 W bulb, which is likely to fuse. In series the larger resistance dissipates more power, so the 25 W bulb dissipates more.
steps: P = I²R: larger in the 1936 Ω bulb → (d) false
solution.why_others_wrong: (d) is false: with the same current in both, P = I²R is four times larger in the 25 W bulb (about 64 W against 16 W). The other codes either include (d) or leave out the true statement (a).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors - series and parallel; electrical energy, power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A charged particle moves in a circle of radius r at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. If its speed is halved and the magnetic field is doubled (the particle still moving at right angles to the field), the radius of its circular path becomes:

solution.concept: Radius of the circular path r = mv/(qB)
solution.explanation: The magnetic force qvB provides the centripetal force mv²/r, so r = mv/(qB): directly proportional to the speed and inversely proportional to the field.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4r inverts the dependence on both v and B. r assumes the two changes cancel, but both make the radius smaller. r/2 applies only one of the two changes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A straight wire 0.50 m long lies along the x-axis and carries a current of 2.0 A in the +x direction. It is in a uniform magnetic field B = (3.0 î + 4.0 ĵ) mT. The magnetic force on the wire is:

solution.concept: Force on a straight current-carrying conductor F = I(l × B)
solution.explanation: Only the component of B perpendicular to the wire exerts a force. The x-component of B is along the wire and gives î × î = 0; the y-component gives î × ĵ = k̂.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.0 × 10⁻³ N uses the full magnitude of B (5.0 mT), including the component parallel to the wire. 3.0 × 10⁻³ N uses the parallel component, which gives no force. The −z direction comes from taking B × l instead of l × B.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: The magnetic field at the centre of a circular loop carrying a steady current is B. The loop is replaced by another single circular loop of twice the radius, carrying three times the current. The magnetic field at its centre is:

solution.concept: Field at the centre of a circular loop B = µ₀I/(2R)
solution.explanation: The field at the centre is proportional to the current and inversely proportional to the radius.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6B multiplies by the factor for the radius instead of dividing by it. 3B/4 treats the field as falling off as 1/R². 2B/3 inverts the result.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field on the axis of a circular current loop

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: An electron moves vertically upwards through a region where a uniform horizontal magnetic field points towards the north. The magnetic force on the electron at that instant points:

solution.concept: Magnetic force F = q(v × B); the charge of the electron is negative
solution.explanation: Take east, north and up as a right-handed set of axes (east × north = up). Then up × north = west, so for a positive charge the force would be towards the west. The electron's charge is negative, which reverses the force.
steps: q = −e reverses it: F towards the east
solution.why_others_wrong: West is the direction for a positive charge. The force cannot be along the field (north), and it must be perpendicular to the velocity, so it cannot be vertical.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The magnitude of a magnetic field is 1 tesla if a charge of 1 C moving at 1 m/s at right angles to the field experiences a force of 1 N.
Statement II: A smaller unit of magnetic field, the gauss, equal to 10⁻⁴ T, is also often used.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Unit of magnetic field: the tesla, from F = qvB sin θ, and the gauss
solution.explanation: From F = qvB sin θ with θ = 90°, B = F/(qv), so 1 T = 1 N/(1 C × 1 m/s) = 1 N s C⁻¹ m⁻¹, which is Statement I. The tesla is a rather large unit; NCERT notes that the non-SI unit gauss, 1 G = 10⁻⁴ T, is also often used, which is Statement II.
steps: I: B = F/(qv sin 90°) → 1 T = 1 N s C⁻¹ m⁻¹ → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are correct, so options saying either is false are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force (unit of magnetic field)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Match each device or definition in List-I with the physical effect on which it is based (List-II).

List-I:
A. Moving-coil galvanometer
B. Velocity selector
C. SI definition of the ampere (based on force between currents)
D. A long current-carrying solenoid used as a magnet

List-II:
I. Force between two parallel current-carrying conductors
II. Torque on a current loop in a magnetic field
III. Electric and magnetic forces on a moving charge balancing each other
IV. Its field outside, at large distances, is the same as that of a bar magnet (a magnetic dipole)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Applications of the magnetic force and torque
solution.explanation: The coil of a moving-coil galvanometer turns because of the torque NIAB on a current loop. In a velocity selector, qE and qvB are equal and opposite for particles of speed E/B. The ampere was defined through the force per unit length between two parallel currents. A solenoid's external field is that of a magnetic dipole, like a bar magnet.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-I interchanges the galvanometer and the ampere definition. B-IV, D-III interchanges the velocity selector and the solenoid. A-III, B-II interchanges the galvanometer and the velocity selector.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', moving coil galvanometer; motion in combined electric and magnetic fields; force between two parallel currents; Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', the bar magnet
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A galvanometer of resistance 90 Ω, shunted by a 10 Ω resistor, works as an ammeter of range 0–10 mA. If the 10 Ω shunt is replaced by a 5 Ω shunt, the range of the ammeter becomes:

solution.concept: Shunt: the galvanometer and the shunt share the current in the inverse ratio of their resistances
solution.explanation: First find the full-scale current I_g of the galvanometer from the original arrangement, then the new total current for which the galvanometer current is again I_g.
steps: 10 mA divides as 10 : 90 between G and S → I_g = 10 × 10/100 = 1 mA
New range: I = I_g(G + S)/S = 1 × (90 + 5)/5 = 19 mA
solution.why_others_wrong: 0–20 mA assumes that halving the shunt doubles the range. 0–5 mA moves the range the wrong way: a smaller shunt takes more current, so the range increases. 0–18 mA counts only the shunt current I_gG/S and leaves out the 1 mA through the galvanometer.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', moving coil galvanometer (conversion into an ammeter)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A proton and an alpha particle enter the same uniform magnetic field with momenta of equal magnitude, each moving at right angles to the field. Taking the mass of the alpha particle as 4 times and its charge as 2 times those of the proton, the ratio of the radii of their paths (r_α : r_p) and the ratio of their periods of revolution (T_α : T_p) are, respectively:

solution.concept: r = p/(qB) and T = 2πm/(qB)
solution.explanation: With the same momentum in the same field, the radius depends only on the charge. The period depends on m/q, which is twice as large for the alpha particle.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 1 for the periods forgets that T depends on m/q, which differs for the two particles. 2 : 1 for the radii uses r ∝ m/q, which holds for equal speeds, not equal momenta. The last option inverts both ratios.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A wire bent into an L-shape, with arms of 3.0 cm and 4.0 cm at right angles to each other, carries a current of 2.0 A. It lies in a plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.50 T. The magnitude of the net magnetic force on the wire is:

solution.concept: Force on a bent wire in a uniform field equals the force on a straight wire joining its ends
solution.explanation: The forces on the two arms, BIl₁ and BIl₂, are perpendicular to each other because the arms are perpendicular. Their resultant is BI√(l₁² + l₂²), the force on a straight wire of length 5.0 cm joining the two ends.
solution.shortcut: In a uniform field, F = BI × (straight-line distance between the ends) = 0.50 × 2.0 × 0.05 N.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.070 N adds the two forces as if they were in the same direction. 0.010 N subtracts them. Zero would hold only for a closed loop, whose ends coincide.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A long solenoid is 50 cm long and is wound in 5 layers, each layer having 400 turns spread evenly along its length. It carries a current of 3.0 A. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnetic field well inside the solenoid, near its middle, is about:

solution.concept: Field inside a long solenoid B = µ₀nI, with n the total number of turns per unit length
solution.explanation: Every layer carries the same current round the same axis, so all 5 × 400 = 2000 turns count. Spread over 0.50 m they give n = 4000 turns per metre.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.0 × 10⁻³ T counts only one layer. 7.5 × 10⁻³ T uses the total number of turns (2000) as if it were the number per metre, ignoring the 0.50 m length. 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ T uses turns per centimetre (40 cm⁻¹) without converting to turns per metre.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', the solenoid

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In a region with uniform electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to each other, charged particles moving perpendicular to both fields with speed E/B pass through undeflected, whatever their charge and mass.
Reason (R): For a particle moving faster than E/B in this region, the electric force on it is larger than the magnetic force.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Velocity selector: qE = qvB
solution.explanation: For the right direction of motion, the electric force qE and the magnetic force qvB act in opposite directions. They balance when v = E/B; q cancels from both sides and m does not appear, so A is true. For v > E/B the magnetic force qvB exceeds qE, so the particle is deflected in the direction of the magnetic force. R reverses this and is false.
steps: Balance: qE = qvB → v = E/B, independent of q and m → A true
For v > E/B: qvB > qE → magnetic force is larger → R false
solution.why_others_wrong: R is false, so the options that call both statements true are wrong; A is true, so the option calling A false is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in combined electric and magnetic fields (velocity selector)
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The SI unit of magnetic dipole moment, A m², can also be written as J T⁻¹.
Reason (R): The potential energy of a magnetic dipole of moment m in a uniform magnetic field B is U = −m·B.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Units of magnetic moment from the energy of a dipole in a field
solution.explanation: Since U = −mB cos θ, the moment m has the unit of energy divided by magnetic field, J T⁻¹. Checking: 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹, so J T⁻¹ = (N m)/(N A⁻¹ m⁻¹) = A m². Both statements are true and R is the relation that gives the unit in A.
steps: J T⁻¹ = N m/(N A⁻¹ m⁻¹) = A m² → A true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, and the unit J T⁻¹ follows directly from the energy expression in R.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', the bar magnet (magnetic dipole in a uniform field)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
The Biot–Savart law for the magnetic field of a current element is compared with Coulomb's law for the electric field of a point charge. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The magnetic field of a current element depends on the angle between the element and the line joining it to the field point, while the electric field of a point charge has no such angular dependence.
(b) Both fields obey the principle of superposition.
(c) The source of the electrostatic field (charge) is a scalar, while the source of the magnetic field (I dl) is a vector.
(d) The magnetic field due to a current element at a point does not depend on the distance of the point from the element.
(e) The magnetic field due to a current element falls off as the inverse cube of the distance.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Biot–Savart law: dB = (µ₀/4π) I dl × r̂/r²
solution.explanation: NCERT compares the two laws. Both fields are long range, falling as 1/r², and both obey superposition. The electrostatic field is produced by a scalar source, the charge q, but the magnetic field by a vector source, I dl. The Biot–Savart field contains sin θ, the angle between dl and r, while the Coulomb field has no such factor.
steps: (a) sin θ factor only in Biot–Savart → true
(c) q scalar, I dl vector → true
solution.why_others_wrong: The field of a current element depends on distance as 1/r², so (d) and (e) are both false; every option containing either of them, or leaving out (c), is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field due to a current element, Biot-Savart law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A long straight wire carries a steady current of 5.0 A. A closed path winds twice round the wire (like two turns of a coil) before closing on itself, always going round in the same sense. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnitude of ∮B·dl along this path is about:

solution.concept: Ampere's circuital law ∮B·dl = µ₀I_enclosed, the current being counted each time the path goes round it
solution.explanation: Each complete turn round the wire contributes µ₀I to the line integral (the integral of B dl over one circle of radius r is B × 2πr = µ₀I, and the same holds for any shape of path going once round). Going round twice in the same sense doubles the result.
steps: One turn round the wire: µ₀I
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.3 × 10⁻⁶ T m counts the current only once. Zero would apply to a path that does not encircle the wire. 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ T m uses µ₀/2π in place of µ₀.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', Ampere's circuital law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A magnetic dipole of moment 0.40 A m² is held in a uniform magnetic field of 0.25 T. The torque acting on it has a magnitude of 0.050 N m. The potential energy of the dipole (taken as −m·B) could be:

solution.concept: Torque τ = mB sin θ and potential energy U = −mB cos θ
solution.explanation: The torque fixes sin θ but not θ itself: both θ = 30° and θ = 150° give sin θ = 0.5. These two orientations have potential energies of opposite sign.
solution.why_others_wrong: −0.087 J only and +0.087 J only each miss one of the two angles allowed by sin θ = 0.5. ±0.050 J takes the magnitude of the energy equal to the magnitude of the torque.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', the bar magnet (magnetic dipole in a uniform magnetic field)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A long horizontal wire, fixed in position, carries a steady current of 50 A. A second long, straight, horizontal wire, parallel to it and directly above it, has a mass of 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ kg per metre and carries a current of 25 A. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ and g = 10 m/s², the upper wire can float in equilibrium (supported only by the magnetic force) at a height above the lower wire of:

options.text: 5.0 cm, with the two currents in the same direction
5.0 cm, with the two currents in opposite directions
2.5 cm, with the two currents in opposite directions
10 cm, with the two currents in opposite directions

solution.concept: Force per unit length between parallel currents f = µ₀I₁I₂/(2πd); antiparallel currents repel
solution.explanation: The magnetic force on the upper wire must be upward, i.e. repulsive, so the currents must be in opposite directions. Its magnitude per metre must equal the weight per metre.
solution.why_others_wrong: Currents in the same direction attract, pulling the upper wire down, so it cannot float. 2.5 cm uses µ₀/4π (10⁻⁷) in place of µ₀/2π. 10 cm uses µ₀/π (4 × 10⁻⁷) in place of µ₀/2π.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', force between two parallel currents
solution.final_answer: Option B: 5.0 cm, with the two currents in opposite directions

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A galvanometer of resistance 100 Ω gives full-scale deflection for a current of 1.0 mA. It is first converted into an ammeter of range 0–1.0 A by a suitable shunt. This ammeter (galvanometer with its shunt) is then to be used as a voltmeter of range 0–10 V. The resistance that must be connected in series with the ammeter is:

solution.concept: Galvanometer conversions: shunt for an ammeter, series resistance for a voltmeter
solution.explanation: The ammeter reaches full scale at 1.0 A. Its own resistance is that of G and the shunt in parallel. To read 10 V at full scale, the total resistance must be 10 V/1.0 A = 10 Ω.
steps: Total resistance needed = 10/1.0 = 10 Ω → series resistance = 10 − 0.10 = 9.9 Ω
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 Ω forgets the 0.10 Ω resistance of the ammeter itself. 9.9 kΩ uses the bare galvanometer's full-scale current (1.0 mA), which no longer applies once the shunt is fitted. 10.1 Ω adds the ammeter resistance instead of subtracting it.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', moving coil galvanometer (conversion into ammeter and voltmeter)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Three long straight wires P, Q and S are perpendicular to the plane of the page. P carries a current 4I out of the page, Q carries 6I into the page and S carries 2I out of the page. Each closed path in List-I lies in the plane of the page and is traversed anticlockwise as seen by the reader. Match each path with the value of ∮B·dl along it (List-II).

List-I:
A. A path enclosing P only
B. A path enclosing P and Q only
C. A path enclosing Q and S only
D. A path enclosing P, Q and S

List-II:
I. −4µ₀I
II. zero
III. +4µ₀I
IV. −2µ₀I

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Ampere's circuital law with the right-hand sign rule for enclosed currents
solution.explanation: For an anticlockwise path (seen by the reader), the right-hand rule makes a current out of the page positive and a current into the page negative. ∮B·dl is µ₀ times the algebraic sum of the enclosed currents; wires outside the path contribute nothing.
solution.why_others_wrong: B-I, C-IV interchanges the values for the two two-wire paths. A-I takes the current out of the page as negative. C-II, D-I interchanges the three-wire path (net current zero) with the Q-and-S path.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', Ampere's circuital law
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: An electron and a proton with equal kinetic energies move at right angles to the same uniform magnetic field. The radius of the electron's circular path is smaller than that of the proton's.
Statement II: In this situation, the magnetic forces on the electron and on the proton have equal magnitudes.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: r = mv/(qB) = √(2mK)/(qB); F = qvB
solution.explanation: For equal kinetic energy K and equal charge magnitude, r = √(2mK)/(eB) is proportional to √m, so the much lighter electron moves in the smaller circle: Statement I is true. The electron's speed, √(2K/m), is larger by the factor √(m_p/m_e) ≈ 43, so the force evB on it is larger: Statement II is false.
steps: r ∝ √m for equal K and |q| → electron's r smaller → I true
v ∝ 1/√m → v_e > v_p → F = evB larger for the electron → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II would be true for equal speeds, not equal kinetic energies.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Two long, straight, parallel wires, 10 cm apart in air, carry steady currents of 5.0 A and 10 A in the same direction. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The force per unit length on each wire is 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ N/m.
(b) The wires attract each other.
(c) The magnitude of the magnetic field at the point midway between the wires is 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ T.
(d) In the plane of the wires, the resultant magnetic field is zero at a point between the wires, about 3.3 cm from the 5.0 A wire.
(e) The 10 A wire experiences a force twice as large as the force on the 5.0 A wire.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Field of a long straight wire B = µ₀I/(2πr); force per unit length µ₀I₁I₂/(2πd)
solution.explanation: The force per unit length is µ₀I₁I₂/(2πd), the same on both wires (Newton's third law), and attractive for currents in the same direction. Between the wires the two fields are opposite, so the field at the midpoint is the difference of the two, and the null point lies nearer the smaller current.
steps: (d) 5/x = 10/(10 − x) → x = 10/3 ≈ 3.3 cm from the 5 A wire → true
(e) the forces are equal and opposite → false
solution.why_others_wrong: (e) is false because the two wires exert equal and opposite forces on each other. The codes with (e), or without (a) or (d), are therefore wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field due to a long straight wire; force between two parallel currents

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A coil of 50 turns, each of area 0.020 m², lies with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.50 T. The direction of the field is reversed (its magnitude staying 0.50 T) in 0.10 s. The magnitude of the average emf induced in the coil is:

solution.concept: Faraday's law: average emf = NΔΦ/Δt
solution.explanation: The flux through each turn changes from +BA to −BA, a change of 2BA, not BA.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.0 V takes the change of flux as BA, as if the field had only been switched off. Zero assumes the flux is unchanged because the magnitude of the field is the same. 20 V counts the change as 4BA.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Faraday's law of induction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The reactance of an ideal inductor of inductance 0.10 H is 31.4 Ω at a certain frequency of the AC source. That frequency is about:

solution.concept: Inductive reactance X_L = ωL = 2πfL
solution.explanation: Solve X_L = 2πfL for f.
solution.why_others_wrong: 314 Hz is the angular frequency ω = X_L/L (in rad/s), not the frequency. 100 Hz leaves out the factor 2. 25 Hz uses 4π in place of 2π.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', AC voltage applied to an inductor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A long straight wire lies in the plane of the page and carries a current directed towards the top of the page. A rectangular conducting loop lies in the same plane, to the right of the wire. The current in the wire is increasing. As seen by a reader looking at the page, the current induced in the loop is:

options.text: zero, because the loop does not move
clockwise in the side nearer the wire only

solution.concept: Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change of flux that produces it
solution.explanation: By the right-hand rule, the field of the upward current is into the page at points to the right of the wire. As the current grows, the inward flux through the loop increases. The induced current must produce an outward field inside the loop, which requires an anticlockwise current.
steps: Field of wire on its right: into the page
Induced field must be out of the page → anticlockwise current
solution.why_others_wrong: Clockwise would add to the increasing inward flux, against Lenz's law. A changing flux induces an emf even in a stationary loop. The current in a single closed loop is the same all round it; it cannot flow in one side only.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Lenz's law and conservation of energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For a given rate of change of magnetic flux through each turn, the emf induced in a closely wound coil is proportional to its number of turns.
Statement II: Lenz's law gives the magnitude of the induced emf, while Faraday's law gives only its direction.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Faraday's law ε = −N dΦ/dt; Lenz's law fixes the direction (the minus sign)
solution.explanation: Statement I is true: the emfs of the N turns add, ε = −N dΦ_B/dt. Statement II reverses the roles: Faraday's law gives the magnitude of the emf, and Lenz's law tells us its polarity (the induced current opposes the change in flux).
steps: I: ε = N dΦ/dt → proportional to N → true
II: the roles are reversed → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II is false because Lenz's law is about the direction, not the magnitude, of the induced emf.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Faraday's law of induction; Lenz's law
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: When the current in a coil rises steadily from 2.0 A to 6.0 A in 0.020 s, a self-induced emf of 20 V appears across it. The self-inductance of the coil is:

solution.concept: Self-induced emf ε = L dI/dt
solution.explanation: The current changes by 6.0 − 2.0 = 4.0 A in 0.020 s, i.e. at 200 A/s.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.20 H uses the initial current (2.0 A) instead of the change in current. 10 H inverts the ratio. 0.067 H uses the final current (6.0 A) instead of the change.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', self-inductance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A metal rod slides along two parallel conducting rails 0.40 m apart, which are joined at one end through a 2.0 Ω resistor; the rod and rails have negligible resistance. A uniform magnetic field of 0.50 T acts at right angles to the plane of the rails. The rod is moved (not necessarily at constant speed) through a distance of 1.0 m along the rails. The total charge that flows through the resistor is:

options.text: It cannot be found without knowing the speed of the rod

solution.concept: Charge driven round a circuit by induction: q = ΔΦ/R, independent of how fast the flux changes
solution.explanation: At each instant I = ε/R = (1/R) dΦ/dt, so the total charge is q = ∫I dt = ΔΦ/R. The flux changes by B × (area swept by the rod) = BLd, however fast or slowly the rod moves.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.20 C is the change of flux in webers, not divided by the resistance. 0.40 C multiplies by R instead of dividing. The speed is not needed, because the charge depends only on the total change of flux.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Faraday's law of induction; motional electromotive force

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In an AC circuit, the voltage applied and the current drawn are v = 100 sin(ωt) volt and i = 5.0 sin(ωt − π/3) ampere. The average power consumed by the circuit is:

solution.concept: Average power P = V_rms I_rms cos φ = ½V₀I₀ cos φ
solution.explanation: The current lags the voltage by φ = π/3, so the power factor is cos 60° = 0.5. The rms values are the peak values divided by √2, so V_rms I_rms = ½V₀I₀.
solution.why_others_wrong: 250 W uses the peak values without the factor ½ (or forgets the power factor). 500 W multiplies the peak values directly. 217 W uses cos 30° instead of cos 60°.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', power in AC circuit: the power factor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The coil of an AC generator has 100 turns, each of area 0.10 m², and rotates at 100 rad/s about an axis perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.10 T. At t = 0 the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field. The magnitude of the emf induced in the coil at the instant when it has turned through 30° from this position is:

solution.concept: Emf of an AC generator ε = NBAω sin ωt, with ωt measured from the position of maximum flux
solution.explanation: With the plane perpendicular to B at t = 0, the flux is Φ = NBA cos ωt and the emf is NBAω sin ωt. The peak emf is NBAω = 100 × 0.10 × 0.10 × 100 = 100 V.
solution.why_others_wrong: 87 V uses cos 30°, which would apply if the angle were measured from the position where the plane is parallel to the field. 100 V is the peak emf, reached only when the plane is parallel to the field. Zero is the emf at t = 0, when the flux is maximum.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', AC generator

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The rms value of a sinusoidal alternating current is larger than its peak value.
Reason (R): For a sinusoidal current of peak value i_m, the rms value is i_m/√2.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: rms (effective) value of a sinusoidal current
solution.explanation: R is the standard result I = i_m/√2 ≈ 0.707 i_m. It shows that the rms value is smaller than the peak value, so A is false.
solution.why_others_wrong: A contradicts R: dividing by √2 makes the rms value about 0.71 of the peak value.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', AC voltage applied to a resistor (rms or effective current)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each quantity in List-I with the way it depends on the frequency of the AC source (List-II).

List-I:
A. Resistance of an ideal resistor
B. Reactance of an ideal inductor
C. Reactance of an ideal capacitor
D. Impedance of a series LCR circuit

List-II:
I. Inversely proportional to the frequency
II. Independent of the frequency
III. Least at the resonant frequency
IV. Directly proportional to the frequency

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: X_L = ωL, X_C = 1/(ωC), Z = √[R² + (X_C − X_L)²]
solution.explanation: A resistance does not depend on frequency. X_L = 2πfL grows in proportion to f, and X_C = 1/(2πfC) falls as 1/f. The impedance of a series LCR circuit is least, equal to R, at the resonant frequency where X_L = X_C.
solution.why_others_wrong: B-I, C-IV interchanges the inductor and the capacitor. A-III, D-II interchanges the resistor and the LCR circuit. A-IV, B-II interchanges the resistor and the inductor.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', AC voltage applied to an inductor; to a capacitor; series LCR circuit
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A 60 Ω resistor and an ideal inductor of reactance 80 Ω are connected in series to a 100 V (rms) AC supply. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The rms current in the circuit is 1.0 A.
(b) The power factor of the circuit is 0.80.
(c) The average power drawn from the supply is 60 W.
(d) The rms voltages across the resistor and across the inductor add up to 100 V.
(e) The current lags behind the supply voltage by the angle tan⁻¹(4/3).

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Series RL circuit: Z = √(R² + X_L²), cos φ = R/Z, tan φ = X_L/R
solution.explanation: Z = √(60² + 80²) = 100 Ω, so I = 1.0 A. The power factor is R/Z = 0.60 and the power is I²R = 60 W. The rms voltages are 60 V and 80 V; they are 90° out of phase, so they add as phasors (√(60² + 80²) = 100 V), not arithmetically. The current lags by φ with tan φ = 80/60 = 4/3.
solution.why_others_wrong: (b) gives sin φ (0.80) instead of cos φ (0.60). (d) adds the rms voltages arithmetically, ignoring their 90° phase difference.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', series LCR circuit; power in AC circuit: the power factor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A power of 1.0 MW is to be sent to a town through transmission lines of total resistance 5.0 Ω. The losses in the lines are calculated first for transmission at 10 kV (rms) and then for transmission at 100 kV (rms), the voltage being raised by a step-up transformer at the power station. Treating the load as drawing current in phase with the voltage, the power lost in the lines in the two cases is, respectively:

solution.concept: Line loss I²R with I = P/V: raising the voltage lowers the current and the loss as 1/V²
solution.explanation: For a fixed power transmitted, the line current is P/V. The loss in the lines is I²R, so a tenfold rise in voltage reduces the current tenfold and the loss a hundredfold.
steps: At 10 kV: I = 10⁶/10⁴ = 100 A; loss = 100² × 5.0 = 5.0 × 10⁴ W = 50 kW (5% of the power)
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 kW and 5.0 kW takes the loss as falling in proportion to 1/V instead of 1/V². 25 kW and 0.25 kW puts a needless factor ½ in, as if the rms current were half the value P/V. 20 MW and 2.0 GW uses V²/R with the transmission voltage, which is not the voltage across the lines.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', transformers (transmission of electrical energy)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The coil of an AC generator has 100 turns, each of area 0.050 m², and rotates at a constant angular speed of 100 rad/s about an axis perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.20 T. Its ends are connected to a 50 Ω resistor; the coil's own resistance and all friction are negligible. The average torque that must be applied to keep the coil rotating at this speed is:

solution.concept: Energy conservation: mechanical power supplied = electrical power dissipated; P = τω
solution.explanation: The peak emf is NBAω. The average power in the resistor is ε₀²/(2R). This power must be supplied by the applied torque, whose average value is P/ω.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 N m uses ε₀²/R, forgetting that the average of sin² over a cycle is ½. 100 N m gives the power in watts as if it were the torque. 0.010 N m divides the power by ω².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', AC generator; Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', power in AC circuit

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A small single-turn circular loop of radius 1.0 cm is placed at the centre of a large single-turn circular loop of radius 20 cm, the two loops being coplanar and concentric. Treating the magnetic field of the large loop as uniform over the small loop, and taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the mutual inductance of the pair is about:

solution.concept: Mutual inductance M = Φ₂/I₁; field at the centre of a loop B = µ₀I/(2R)
solution.explanation: A current I₁ in the large loop gives a field µ₀I₁/(2R) at its centre, which is nearly uniform over the small loop. The flux through the small loop is this field times its area πr².
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ H uses µ₀I/R for the field at the centre (factor 2 missing). 4.9 × 10⁻¹⁰ H uses µ₀I/(4R). 3.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ H takes the area of the small loop as r² instead of πr².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', mutual inductance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A long air-cored solenoid has self-inductance L. It is rewound so that its total number of turns is doubled, its length is doubled and its radius is halved (it stays long compared with its radius). Its new self-inductance is:

solution.concept: Self-inductance of a long solenoid L = µ₀n²Al = µ₀N²πr²/l
solution.explanation: Write L in terms of the total number of turns N: with n = N/l, L = µ₀(N/l)²(πr²)l = µ₀N²πr²/l.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2L ignores the change of radius. L ignores the change of length. L/4 takes L as proportional to N instead of N².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', self-inductance (long solenoid)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each quantity in List-I with its expression in List-II. (n, n₁, n₂ = turns per unit length; A = area of cross-section; l = length; r₁ = radius of the inner solenoid; B = magnetic field in vacuum.)

List-I:
A. Self-inductance of a long solenoid
B. Mutual inductance of two long coaxial solenoids of length l
C. Magnetic energy stored in an inductor L carrying current I
D. Magnetic energy per unit volume of a field B

List-II:
I. B²/(2µ₀)
II. µ₀n²Al
III. ½LI²
IV. µ₀n₁n₂πr₁²l

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Inductance of solenoids and magnetic energy
solution.explanation: For a long solenoid, Φ per turn = µ₀nIA and N = nl, so L = µ₀n²Al. For coaxial solenoids, the field µ₀n₂I₂ of the outer one links the n₁l turns of the inner one over area πr₁², giving M = µ₀n₁n₂πr₁²l. The work done against the self-induced emf in building up a current I is ½LI². Dividing ½LI² for a solenoid by its volume Al gives the energy density B²/(2µ₀).
solution.why_others_wrong: A-IV, B-II interchanges self- and mutual inductance. C-I, D-III interchanges the total energy and the energy per unit volume. A-III, C-II interchanges the inductance and the energy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', inductance (self-inductance and mutual inductance)
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: According to NCERT, the radiation focused through a laser in LASIK (laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis) eye surgery belongs to the:

solution.concept: Uses of different parts of the electromagnetic spectrum
solution.explanation: NCERT notes that ultraviolet radiation can be focused into very narrow beams for high-precision applications such as LASIK eye surgery.
steps: UV can be focused into very narrow beams → used in LASIK
solution.why_others_wrong: Infrared is used in remote switches and physical therapy, microwaves in radar and ovens, and gamma rays to destroy cancer cells; none of these is the radiation NCERT names for LASIK.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic spectrum (ultraviolet rays)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A radio station broadcasts at a frequency of 1.5 MHz. Taking the speed of electromagnetic waves in air as 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, the wavelength of the waves is:

solution.concept: c = fλ for electromagnetic waves
solution.explanation: All electromagnetic waves travel at c in vacuum (and very nearly in air), so λ = c/f.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.20 m treats 1.5 MHz as 1.5 GHz. 4.5 × 10¹⁴ m multiplies c by f. 2.0 × 10⁵ m takes MHz as kHz.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic waves (speed c = fλ)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: At a certain point and instant, the electric field of a plane electromagnetic wave travelling in vacuum has a magnitude of 30 V/m and points along +z, while its magnetic field points along +x. Taking c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, the magnitude of the magnetic field and the direction of propagation of the wave are:

solution.concept: In a plane EM wave B₀ = E₀/c, and the wave travels along E × B
solution.explanation: E, B and the direction of propagation are mutually perpendicular, and the propagation is along E × B. Here ẑ × x̂ = ŷ.
steps: Direction of propagation: E × B = ẑ × x̂ = +ŷ
solution.why_others_wrong: −y comes from taking B × E instead of E × B. 9.0 × 10⁹ T multiplies E by c. The wave cannot travel along +z, the direction of its own electric field, because the wave is transverse.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic waves (nature of electromagnetic waves)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Gamma rays are used in medicine to destroy cancer cells.
Statement II: Visible light occupies the wavelength range from about 100 nm to 400 nm.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Uses and wavelength ranges of parts of the electromagnetic spectrum
solution.explanation: Statement I is true: NCERT lists the destruction of cancer cells as a medical use of gamma rays. Statement II is false: visible light extends from about 400 nm to about 700 nm; wavelengths shorter than about 400 nm are ultraviolet.
steps: I: gamma rays destroy cancer cells → true
solution.why_others_wrong: The range in Statement II belongs to the ultraviolet, not to visible light.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic spectrum
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): While a capacitor is being charged, there is a magnetic field in the gap between its plates, although no charge flows across the gap.
Reason (R): A changing electric flux produces a magnetic field in the same way as a conduction current does; Maxwell called the term ε₀ dΦ_E/dt the displacement current.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Ampere–Maxwell law: ∮B·dl = µ₀(i_c + ε₀ dΦ_E/dt)
solution.explanation: No conduction current crosses the gap, but the electric field between the plates grows as the capacitor charges, so the electric flux through the gap changes. By the Ampere–Maxwell law this displacement current is a source of magnetic field, just like a conduction current, which is why there is a magnetic field in the gap. R is the reason for A.
steps: A: magnetic field exists in the gap → true
R: dΦ_E/dt term acts as a source of B → true
The changing flux in the gap is what produces that field → R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: Both are true and the displacement current of R is precisely the source of the field described in A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', displacement current
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each electromagnetic wave in List-I, given by its frequency, with the part of the spectrum to which it belongs (List-II). Take c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s and use the wavelength ranges given in NCERT.

List-I:
A. 100 MHz
B. 10 GHz
C. 6 × 10¹⁴ Hz
D. 3 × 10¹⁸ Hz

List-II:
I. Visible light
II. X-rays
III. Radio waves
IV. Microwaves

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: λ = c/f, then compare with the wavelength ranges of the spectrum
solution.explanation: Convert each frequency to a wavelength: 100 MHz → 3 m (radio, > 0.1 m); 10 GHz → 3 cm (microwaves, 0.1 m to 1 mm); 6 × 10¹⁴ Hz → 500 nm (visible, about 400–700 nm); 3 × 10¹⁸ Hz → 0.1 nm (X-rays, about 10 nm to 10⁻⁴ nm).
solution.why_others_wrong: A-IV, B-III interchanges radio waves and microwaves (the higher frequency is the microwave). C-II, D-I interchanges visible light and X-rays. A-IV, B-I, C-III scrambles the order of increasing frequency.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic spectrum
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A reflecting telescope has a concave objective mirror of radius of curvature 4.0 m and an eyepiece of focal length 2.0 cm. Its magnifying power in normal adjustment is:

solution.concept: Magnifying power of a telescope in normal adjustment m = f_o/f_e; for a mirror f = R/2
solution.explanation: The objective mirror has focal length R/2 = 2.0 m = 200 cm. The magnifying power is f_o/f_e.
solution.why_others_wrong: 200 uses the radius of curvature as the focal length. 50 halves the result twice. 0.01 is f_e/f_o, the ratio inverted.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', optical instruments (telescope)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Light falls normally on a glass plate 3.0 mm thick, of refractive index 1.5. Taking the speed of light in vacuum as 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, the time taken by the light to cross the plate is:

solution.concept: Speed of light in a medium v = c/n
solution.explanation: In the glass the light travels at c/n = 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s, so it takes longer than in vacuum to cover the same thickness.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ s uses the speed in vacuum. 2.25 × 10⁻¹¹ s multiplies by n twice. 6.7 × 10⁻¹² s uses nc instead of c/n, as if light were faster in glass.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In Huygens' construction, each point of a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets, but only the forward envelope of the wavelets is taken as the new wavefront. NCERT justifies ignoring the backward wave by:

options.text: assuming that the amplitude of the secondary wavelets is maximum in the forward direction and zero in the backward direction
the fact that light cannot travel backwards in any medium
assuming that the secondary wavelets travel faster in the forward direction
the destructive interference of the backward wavelets with the incident wave, which Huygens proved

solution.concept: Huygens' principle and its ad hoc assumption about the backwave
solution.explanation: NCERT notes that a backwave is not observed, and that Huygens explained its absence by assuming the amplitude of the secondary wavelets to be maximum in the forward direction and zero in the backward direction. This is an ad hoc assumption that gives the right result; the backwave is properly removed only by a more rigorous wave theory.
steps: Huygens: amplitude of secondary wavelets zero in the backward direction (ad hoc)
solution.why_others_wrong: Light can of course travel in any direction (reflection sends it back). The wavelets travel at the same speed in all directions in a uniform medium. Huygens gave no interference proof; the assumption is ad hoc.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', Huygens principle
solution.final_answer: Option A: assuming that the amplitude of the secondary wavelets is maximum in the forward direction and zero in the backward direction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two coherent light waves of the same wavelength λ and equal intensity, coming from in-phase sources, meet at a point with a phase difference of 3π. The path difference between them and the nature of the point are:

options.text: 3λ/4; a point of intensity half the maximum

solution.concept: Phase difference φ = (2π/λ) × path difference; intensity I = 4I₀ cos²(φ/2)
solution.explanation: A phase difference of 2π corresponds to a path difference of λ, so 3π corresponds to 3λ/2, an odd multiple of λ/2. The waves are in opposite phase and, having equal intensities, cancel completely.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3λ uses Δx = φλ/π. An odd multiple of λ/2 gives destructive, not constructive, interference. 3λ/4 halves the path difference again.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', coherent and incoherent addition of waves; interference
solution.final_answer: Option C: 3λ/2; a dark point (zero intensity)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ray of light falls on a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of 30°. The angle through which the ray is deviated from its original direction by the reflection is:

solution.concept: Law of reflection; deviation by a plane mirror δ = 180° − 2i
solution.explanation: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, 30°. The incident and reflected rays make an angle of 2i = 60° with each other measured through the normal, so the reflected ray is turned through 180° − 60° from the original direction of travel.
steps: Angle between incident and reflected rays (through the normal) = 2i = 60°
solution.why_others_wrong: 60° is the angle between the incident and reflected rays, not the deviation. 30° is the angle of reflection. 150° uses 180° − i.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', reflection of light by spherical mirrors (laws of reflection)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match the refractive index of each transparent medium in List-I with the speed of light in it (List-II). Take the speed of light in vacuum as 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

List-I:
A. 1.5
B. 4/3
C. 2.0
D. 1.25

List-II:
I. 1.5 × 10⁸ m/s
II. 2.4 × 10⁸ m/s
III. 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s
IV. 2.25 × 10⁸ m/s

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Absolute refractive index n = c/v
solution.explanation: The speed in each medium is c/n: the larger the refractive index, the smaller the speed.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-IV, B-III interchanges the values for 1.5 and 4/3. C-II, D-I interchanges those for 2.0 and 1.25. A-I, C-III gives the medium of index 2.0 a larger speed than that of index 1.5.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin glass lens (refractive index 1.5) has one convex surface of radius of curvature 20 cm and one concave surface of radius of curvature 30 cm, the centres of curvature of both surfaces lying on the same side of the lens (a converging meniscus). Its focal length in air is:

solution.concept: Lens maker's formula 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂) with the Cartesian sign convention
solution.explanation: With light going left to right and both centres of curvature on the right, R₁ = +20 cm and R₂ = +30 cm.
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 cm treats the lens as biconvex (adds 1/20 and 1/30). 60 cm leaves out the factor (n − 1) = 0.5. −120 cm has the sign wrong: the more strongly curved surface is the convex one, so the lens converges.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction by a lens (lens maker's formula)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An object and a screen are fixed a certain distance apart, and a convex lens placed between them forms a sharp image on the screen at two different positions of the lens. The heights of the two images are 9.0 cm and 4.0 cm. The height of the object is:

solution.concept: Conjugate positions: the object and image distances interchange, so m₁m₂ = 1
solution.explanation: In the two positions u and v are interchanged, so the magnifications are v/u and u/v, whose product is 1. Hence h₁h₂ = h², the object height being the geometric mean of the image heights.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.5 cm is the arithmetic mean of the image heights. 5.0 cm is their difference. 2.25 cm is their ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction by a lens; magnification

questions.subject: Physics
